seoTitle: Free PKCE Generator: code_verifier and S256 Challenge
metaDescription: Generate an RFC 7636 PKCE code_verifier, its S256 code_challenge, plus random state and nonce. Free, and everything runs in your browser.
intro: Create a PKCE code_verifier and its S256 code_challenge for OAuth, with a random state and nonce. You can also paste your own verifier to get its challenge.
why:
PKCE protects the OAuth authorisation code flow for public clients such as single-page apps and mobile apps. The client invents a secret verifier, sends only its SHA-256 hash in the authorisation request, and later proves it owns the secret when exchanging the code.

While you are integrating with an identity provider, it helps to produce a matching pair by hand and test the endpoints with curl or Postman. This tool makes a verifier of 43 to 128 characters from the allowed set, hashes it with SHA-256 using your browser crypto API, and encodes the result as Base64URL. In a real app, generate a fresh verifier for every login request in code; do not reuse values from a web page.
howTo: Choose a verifier length between 43 and 128, or paste your own verifier.
Read the code_verifier, code_challenge, method, state and nonce.
Use the challenge in the authorise request and the verifier in the token request.

faq.a: RFC 7636 recommends S256 whenever the client can compute SHA-256, and the plain method offers little protection. The tool outputs code_challenge_method=S256.

faq.q: What characters can a verifier contain?
faq.a: Letters, digits, hyphen, dot, underscore and tilde, with a length of 43 to 128. A pasted value outside this rule is rejected with an error.

faq.q: Should I use generated values in production?
faq.a: No. Use them to test and learn the flow. A real client should generate a new random verifier per authorisation request, in code, and keep it only in memory or session storage until the token exchange.

faq.q: What are state and nonce for?
faq.a: State ties the response to your request and defends against cross-site request forgery. Nonce, used with OpenID Connect, ties the ID token to the request and defends against replay.
